title: Pranzini (1887)
hook: the comments under a trial all say 'hope he rots'; Thérèse prays for a condemned murderer she never met
tomorrow: can a teenager just walk up and ask the pope for something?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a staircase, and a girl who chose not to cry. The line was strength came at christmas.
screen: `STRENGTH CAME AT CHRISTMAS.` → `NOW, A CONDEMNED MAN.`

segments.voice: A trial is all over the news, and the comments under it say the same thing over and over: hope he rots. In France, a man named Pranzini is condemned to die for terrible murders, and everything Thérèse hears says he's unrepentant. She has never met him. She decides he will not be lost, and starts to pray for him, quietly, telling almost no one.
screen: `HOPE HE ROTS.` → `CONDEMNED, AND UNREPENTANT.` → `SHE DECIDES HE WON'T BE LOST.`

segments.voice: Why him? Not long before, a picture of Jesus on the cross had struck her: blood falling from his hand, and no one hurrying to catch it. Jesus's cry, in the Douay-Rheims, "I thirst," lit in her a thirst for souls. So she prays for Pranzini, offers small sacrifices, and asks her sister Céline to have a Mass said for him. She asks God for a sign, just for her comfort. Then a newspaper: at the scaffold, without having made his confession, Pranzini suddenly turned, took the crucifix the priest held out, and kissed its wounds. She calls him her first child. Praying for him doesn't erase what he did, or the people he harmed. It refuses to decide that anyone is beyond reach. A neighbor tradition carries that same hope. In a Buddhist sutta, Angulimala, a bandit feared for his killings, meets the Buddha, turns, and becomes a monk. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says: "He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." Shared: nobody is written off. The honest difference: Thérèse's hope rests on God's mercy, asked for by someone else in prayer. Angulimala turns through his own practice on the Buddha's path, and when people throw stones at him, he is told he's bearing the fruit of his own deeds.
screen: `I THIRST: A THIRST FOR SOULS.` · `HE KISSED THE CRUCIFIX.` · `ANGULIMALA TURNS.` · `ONE HOPE, TWO WAYS IT COMES.` · then, large: `MY FIRST CHILD.`

segments.voice: Say out loud, quietly, the first name of one person in prison, someone you know or someone you've only read about, and then: and the people they hurt. Hold them all for a moment without deciding what anyone deserves. If you pray, you can place them before God, as Thérèse did.
Pranzini. A condemned murderer Thérèse prayed for, who kissed the crucifix before he died.
Remember this one: my first child, because for Thérèse nobody was too far away to pray for. Until next time.

screen: `DAY 1525 COUNTS.` → `STORY OF A SOUL · 9 OF 20.` → `TOMORROW: CAN A TEENAGER JUST ASK THE POPE?`

howItsDone: Catholics pray for prisoners and for the dying, and visiting the imprisoned is one of the corporal works of mercy; some parishes run prison ministries.

fork.setup: in world history, your class reads about Angulimala, and someone says, so it's the same story as Thérèse and Pranzini. what's the honest answer?
options: both refuse to write a person off; they differ on how the turn comes.
exactly the same story, just told in two religions.
nothing alike: one is about a monk, one about a criminal.
fork.reveal: both hold that a life that did terrible harm can still turn. Thérèse trusts God's mercy asked in prayer; Angulimala turns through his own practice, and still bears his deeds' fruit.

chat.says: team chat about that trial is all 'hope he rots.' i get it. but is praying for him weird?
options: Not weird. Thérèse prayed for a condemned man; pray for the people he hurt too.
A bit. Praying for him is like saying what he did doesn't matter.
Only if he's sorry first. Prayer is for people who already repented.
chat.meaning: Thérèse prayed for Pranzini while he seemed unrepentant, without excusing his crimes. For her, nobody was beyond the reach of prayer.
